1:1: This phrase, in the land, refers to the land of Israel.
1:2: The term Ephrathites refers to the people from the clan of Ephrathah, people who lived in the area around Bethlehem.
1:4: The phrase took wives for themselves is an idiom that means that they married women. They did not take women by force or take women who were already married to other men.
1:6: It is implied that the news came from Israel.
1:8: יעשה יְהוָה עִמָּכֶם חֶסֶד כַּאֲשֶׁר עֲשִׂיתֶם עִם־הַמֵּתִים וְעִמָּדִי
Naomi is asking God to bless Orpah and Ruth.
1:9: The word rest here does not refer to sitting down to rest. It means a place where these women would belong, a home for them, which would include the security that comes through marriage.

This means with new husbands, not with their previous husbands, who died, or with someone else’s husband. The word house refers to both a physical house that belongs to the husband and to the protection from shame and poverty that a husband provides.
To lift up the voice is an idiom for speaking or crying loudly.
1:11: Orpah and Ruth are Naomi’s daughters-in-law, but here and in the next two verses she calls them my daughters as a term of affection.
Naomi is using the question form here to convince the young women of her own conviction.
הַעוֹד־לִי בָנִים בְּמֵעַי וְהָיוּ לָכֶם לַאֲנָשִׁים
Naomi is using the question form to make the point that she cannot have other sons for the young women to marry.
1:12: The implication is that Naomi cannot again marry and provide them with husbands.
This rhetorical question begins here and continues into the next verse. Naomi uses this question to emphasize that she cannot provide other sons for them to marry.
1:13: Naomi completes the rhetorical question she began in the previous verse and immediately asks another rhetorical question which emphasizes the same meaning.
This idea refers to the custom among the ancient Hebrews that, if a married man died, one of his brothers would marry the man’s widow. See the book introduction for more explanation.
Here, bitterness is a metaphor for grief.
The implication is that the Lord caused the deaths of Naomi’s family.
1:14: Here, they lifted up their voices is an idiom meaning that they expressed themselves loudly.
This could mean: (1) Ruth refused to leave Naomi; or (2) Ruth physically held on to Naomi and would not let go of her.
1:15: Naomi is using the term Behold to focus Ruth’s attention on what she is about to say.
1:16: The phrase turn back from behind you further defines the phrase forsake you. Ruth is using the two phrases together for emphasis.
1:17: כֹּה יַעֲשֶׂה יְהוָה לִי וְכֹה יֹסִיף

Ruth uses this oath formula to show that she is very committed to doing what she says. She calls down a curse on herself, asking God to punish her if she does not do what she has said she would do. In keeping with the custom, she did not express what that punishment would be.

This could mean: (1) even death cannot overcome Ruth’s commitment to Naomi. This could be a form of hyperbole or simply a way to restate her commitment to be buried in the same place as Naomi is buried; (2) the only thing that can separate Ruth from Naomi would be the death of one of them.
1:18: In this phrase, she refers to Naomi, and her refers to Ruth. Also, this does not mean that Naomi was angry with Ruth or that she no longer spoke to her at all. It only means that she stopped trying to persuade Ruth to leave her.
1:19: Here, town represents the people who live there.
The word entire here is a generalization for emphasis. Many of the residents of the town were excited, but not all of the residents may have been excited by this news.

The writer is using a rhetorical question to emphasize the reaction of the people to Naomi’s condition upon her return. Because it had been many years since Naomi lived in Bethlehem and now she no longer has her husband and two sons, it is likely that the women were expressing shock that this woman was actually Naomi.
1:21: אֲנִי מְלֵאָה הָלַכְתִּי וְרֵיקָם הֱשִׁיבַנִי יְהוָה
Here, Naomi is speaking of herself as a container that can be full or empty.
Naomi is using the question form to emphasize that there is no reason to call her Naomi.
וַיהוָה עָנָה בִי וְשַׁדַּי הֵרַע לִי
These two statements say the same thing using different words to emphasize the idea that God has made Naomi’s life very hard. Both The Lord and the Almighty refer to God.
Here Naomi is speaking of The Lord as if he were a witness who caused her to be punished for a crime.
1:22: וְהֵמָּה בָּאוּ בֵּית לֶחֶם בִּתְחִלַּת קְצִיר שְׂעֹרִים
This sentence provides background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story.
2:1: Verse 1 gives background information about Boaz so that the reader will understand who he is.
The expression a man of great worth describes Boaz as a person who was prosperous and well known in his community, with a good reputation. See the chapter introduction for more information.

The use of the term clan here means that Boaz was related to Elimelek but did not have the same parents as Elimelek. The text is not saying that the clan was named after Elimelek or that Elimelek was the patriarch or leader of the clan, but only that Elimelek and Boaz belonged to the same clan.
2:2: The idiom in whose eyes I find favor means “whoever will approve of me.” Ruth speaks of gaining someone’s favor as gaining permission, kindness, or approval.
Ruth was caring for Naomi as if she were her own mother, and Naomi addressed Ruth affectionately as her daughter.
2:3: The phrase, her chance chanced upon indicates that Ruth did not know whose field she was in.

The use of the term clan here means that Boaz was related to Elimelek but did not have the same parents as Elimelek. The text is not saying that the clan was named after Elimelek or that Elimelek was the patriarch or leader of the clan.
2:4: The writer is using the term behold to alert us to the important event of Boaz arriving at the field and seeing Ruth for the first time.
2:5: In that culture, women were under the authority of their male relatives. Boaz was asking whom Ruth’s husband or father might be. He did not think that Ruth was a slave.
2:6: The two words answered and said express a single idea.
2:7: The two words glean and gather express a single idea.
Here, the house was a temporary shelter or garden hut in the field that provided shade from the sun where the workers could rest.
2:8: Boaz is using the question form to draw Ruth’s attention to what he will say to her.
Boaz’s use of the term, my daughter was a kind way to address a younger woman. Ruth was not the actual daughter of Boaz, but he was treating her kindly and respectfully.
2:9: Here, the word eyes represents the capability of a person to see, watch or observe.
Here, them is feminine and refers back to the “young female workers” in verse 8.
Boaz is using the question form to emphasize his hospitality—that he had already made provision to help Ruth.
The writer assumes that his readers will understand the implications of a woman toiling in a field near young male workers.
The writer is referring to harm or sexual assault in a polite way by using the phrase touch you.
2:10: These are two descriptions of a single action. The writer may be using the two terms together for emphasis.

The action of falling on her face and bowing down to the ground was a symbol of respect and reverence. She was showing honor to Boaz out of gratefulness for what he had done for her. It was also a posture of humility.
The idiom fell on her face means that she bowed low with her face to the ground.
Ruth speaks of Boaz’s kindness to her as his favor or approval of her.
2:11: Both answered and said describe the same action.
With the words you came to a people, Boaz is referring to Ruth coming to dwell with Naomi in a village and community, a country and religion that she did not know.
2:12: The implication is that her work was the good things she had done, everything Boaz had just described.
This clause and the previous clause mean basically the same thing. The second clause emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
Here, under whose wings is a metaphor that uses the picture of a mother bird gathering her chicks under her wings to protect them as a way to describe God’s protection for those who trust in him.
2:13: Here, the heart represents the inner thoughts and emotions of a person.
2:14: This was a simple meal eaten in the field. People would sit on the ground around a cloth that had a bowl of wine vinegar on it and pieces of broken bread. They would take a piece of bread and dip it in the wine vinegar to add flavor before they ate it. The Israelites made vinegar from grape juice that was fermented beyond the point of being wine. At the vinegar stage, the juice becomes very sour and acidic.
2:15: When Boaz spoke to his workers, it is likely that Ruth was far enough away that she did not hear Boaz’s instructions.

Here, the word even lets the workers know that they are to do above and beyond what they normally do. People who were gleaning were normally forbidden from working close to the harvested grain because then it would be easy for them to steal from the grain that was already harvested. But Boaz instructs his workers to let Ruth glean close to the bundles of harvested grain.
Boaz is referring to shaming Ruth by scolding her verbally.
2:16: Here Boaz goes another step beyond what is normal and tells his workers to also drop on the ground some of the grain that they had harvested for Ruth to pick up.
2:17: Ruth would have beaten the barley stalks with a big stick until the kernels of edible grain came off. She would then keep only the kernels of grain.
An ephah is a unit of measurement equal to about 22 liters.
2:18: It is implied that Ruth carried the grain home.
2:19: Naomi asked the same thing in two different ways to show that she was very excited and interested in knowing what had happened to Ruth that day.
The writer is using the term noticed to mean that the person not only saw Ruth but also did something kind for her.

These two sentences mean basically the same thing. The second sentence repeats the meaning of the first, while using different words in order to emphasize the importance of this information for the story.
2:20: Here, who could refer to: (1) The Lord, who has continued to be faithful to the living and the dead by acting through Boaz. (2) Boaz, who is showing faithfulness to Naomi’s family by helping Ruth.
These two sentences mean basically the same thing. The second sentence repeats the meaning of the first using different words in order to emphasize the importance of this information for the story.

A kinsman-redeemer was a close male relative who had the responsibility to take care of any widows in the family. If one of his brothers died childless, he had the responsibility to marry the widow if she was still of child-bearing age, to raise a child for his brother. He would also reacquire the land his relatives had lost due to poverty and redeem family members who had sold themselves into slavery. See the book introduction for more information.
2:21: The implication is that what follows is beyond what anyone would have expected a landowner to say to Ruth.
The implication is that Boaz wants to protect and provide for Ruth. Boaz was expressing confidence that his workers would not harm Ruth.
3:1: Naomi is the mother of Ruth’s dead husband, and thus, is Ruth’s mother-in-law.
Ruth became Naomi’s daughter-in-law by marrying Naomi’s son. But here Naomi calls her My daughter to show that she loves her as much as she would love her own daughter.
Naomi is using the question form to cause Ruth to think of her future. Here, Naomi uses this question to tell Ruth what she plans to do.

Here, Naomi is speaking of a permanent home as a resting place. This does not mean a place to rest temporarily from being tired. It means a place of permanent comfort and security in a good home with a husband.
3:2: הֲלֹא בֹעַז מֹדַעְתָּנוּ אֲשֶׁר הָיִית אֶת־נַעֲרוֹתָיו
Naomi uses the question form here to remind Ruth of something she had already told her (See 2:20).
The implication is that Boaz owned the fields where Ruth worked together with these young women, not that Boaz owned the young women.
Naomi is using the term Behold to focus Ruth’s attention on what she is about to say.
3:3: A threshing floor is an open, flat area where workers could thresh and winnow grain. It would be outside of the city, which was high on a hill, and thus, one would go “down” to it.
3:4: To uncover his feet means to remove the cloak or blanket covering his feet, and probably also his legs. This action by a woman was probably a symbolic action that was interpreted as a proposal of marriage.
The word translated feet could be used as a euphemism for a man’s private parts, but here it refers to the man’s feet or legs.
וְהוּא יַגִּיד לָךְ אֵת אֲשֶׁר תַּעַשִׂין
The specific custom of that time is unclear, but Naomi appears to believe that Boaz will understand Ruth’s action as a proposal of marriage. Boaz will then either accept or reject her offer.
Here, the word himself emphasizes that Boaz will decide what happens next, not Naomi or Ruth.
3:7: Here heart stands for “emotions” or “disposition.” Boaz’s emotions or feelings were good. This does not imply that Boaz was drunk.
3:8: This clause gives information about when the next event in the story happened.
3:10: Boaz uses this phrase again here to communicate kindness and respect from a man to a younger woman.

By marrying Naomi’s relative who is a kinsman-redeemer, Ruth would also provide for Naomi, honor Naomi’s son, and continue Naomi’s family line. Boaz considers this to be Ruth’s greatest demonstration of faithfulness to Naomi.
Boaz is using the phrase at the beginning to refer to the way that Ruth had earlier provided for her mother-in-law by staying with her and gleaning grain for food for both of them.

Boaz is praising Ruth for not going after the young men, by which he means that Ruth could have ignored Naomi’s need and looked for a young and handsome husband for herself outside of Elimelek’s relatives, but she did not.
3:11: Boaz uses this expression as a sign of kindness and respect toward Ruth as a younger woman.
Here, gate represents the people who gather at the gate. The gate was an area of the city where people gathered to do business, and the leaders met there to make decisions.
3:12: This term refers to the male relative who was closest in family relationship to a man who died and who had the responsibility to help his widow.
3:13: The implication of the word redeem is that in this culture it means “marry according to our custom concerning widows.” Boaz is referring to the expectation that the closest male relative of Ruth’s dead husband would marry her and raise a son to carry on the dead man’s family name.
Boaz uses the word myself to emphasize that he was committed to taking care of Ruth.
The phrase as the Lord lives is an oath formula. This was a common Hebrew vow that obligated the speaker to perform what he said.
3:14: The implication of So she lay at his feet is that although Ruth and Boaz were alone together all night, they did not sin sexually.
The idiom before a man could recognize his friend means that it was very early in the morning, before there was enough light to recognize the face of a familiar person.
3:15: A cloak was a long, thick outer garment usually made of cloth.
Many ancient manuscripts read he went, referring to Boaz. Other ancient manuscripts read “she went,” referring to Ruth.
3:16: Naomi’s question to Ruth, “Who are you, my daughter?” appears to be an idiom that probably asks about her current status. In other words, it is likely that Naomi is asking if Ruth is now betrothed to be married.
Ruth is actually Naomi’s daughter-in-law, but Naomi calls her my daughter as an endearment.
Most of what the man had done for her was verbal.
3:17: To go empty is an idiom that means to go to someone with nothing to offer that person.
3:18: Here, Sit is an idiom that means to wait patiently and calmly.
Naomi is using a figure of speech here that expresses a strongly positive meaning by using a negative word, not, together with rest, which is the opposite of the intended meaning.
Here, this matter refers to the need of the two women for a kinsman-redeemer.
4:1: The original readers knew that the gate was the place inside the entrance to the town where community business was publicly conducted.
The writer is using the term behold to focus our attention on the important event of Boaz seeing the exact person whom he wanted to see walking by.
The term kinsman-redeemer specifically refers to the closest living male relative to Elimelek.

Boaz did not actually say a certain person; instead, he called the kinsman-redeemer by his name. This is an idiom that means a specific person, but the name is not given. The narrator has substituted this general term for the person’s name either because he did not want to give the specific name or because the man’s name had been forgotten.
4:3: Here the term brother is used in the broad sense to mean a male relative of an extended family.
4:4: Here, said refers to something that Boaz said to himself in his own mind.
Having these men as witnesses would make the transaction legal and binding.
Here, Boaz is asking about the man’s willingness to redeem the property.
The man uses the word myself here to emphasize that he will do it and no one else.
4:5: Boaz is using one part of a person, the hand of Naomi, to represent Naomi herself and her legal possession of the land.
Boaz is using the term acquire to mean that the man must marry the Moabite woman.
4:6: Here, I damage my own inheritance means that if the man marries Ruth, the property that he buys would belong to her son, not to his own children. In that way, he would be taking away from the wealth that his own children would inherit from him and giving it instead to the children that Ruth might bear.
4:7: The word Now marks what follows as background information that the writer wants the reader to know in order to understand the story.
The word formerly implies that this custom was no longer practiced when the book of Ruth was written. Use a word or phrase that has this meaning.
The words to his friend refer to the person with whom a man was making the agreement.
4:8: The writer assumes that his readers will understand that the kinsman-redeemer gave the sandal to Boaz.
4:9: Here, to the elders and to all the people refers to all the people who were present at the meeting place, not to everyone in the town. The writer uses it here as a generalization for emphasis.
The hand of Naomi represents Naomi. Since her husband and sons had died, the right to the property belonged to her.
4:10: This connecting phrase indicates that the people sitting at the gate are also witnesses to what follows.
וְלֹא־יִכָּרֵת שֵׁם־הַמֵּת מֵעִם אֶחָיו וּמִשַּׁעַר מְקוֹמוֹ
Being forgotten is spoken of here as if one’s name were being cut off from a list of one’s people.
Here, the gate refers to the location where the leaders gathered and made important legal decisions for his place, which refers to his town. This location represents the people there.
4:11: The implication is that the people who were in the gate are the same people who heard and observed the meeting between Boaz and the man who had been first as kinsman-redeemer.

This has both a literal and a figurative meaning. As Ruth marries Boaz, she will move into his physical house. “House” can be a metonym that represents “family,” so this also refers to becoming part of Boaz’s family by being his wife.
Here, the people are asking God to bless Ruth. Their blessing continues for Ruth and Boaz through verse 12.
כְּרָחֵל ׀ וּכְלֵאָה אֲשֶׁר בָּנוּ שְׁתֵּיהֶם אֶת־בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל

Rachel and Leah are the names of two women, the two wives of Jacob, whose name was changed to Israel. They are considered to be the female ancestors of the people of Israel. They had many children, so implied in this blessing is the request that God give Ruth many children.
Here the people are speaking of the nation of Israel as if it were a house.

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. The area around the town of Bethlehem was known as Ephrathah, and that became another name for the town. Presumably, this name came from the Israelite clan that settled in and around the city of Bethlehem.
4:12: Here, house represents the people who might live in a house plus all of their descendants. Perez had many descendants who became large clans in Israel, including the clan of Ephrathah. Also, many of his descendants became important people.
The people are asking for a blessing from the Lord, that through Ruth he would give Boaz many children who would do good things, just as the Lord did for Perez.
4:13: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second clause emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
The phrase, he went in to her is a polite way of referring to sexual intercourse.
4:14: These are the women of the town as mentioned in 1:19.
The women are praising God for what he has done for Naomi and Ruth.
This is a blessing, stating that the women desire that Naomi’s grandson will have a good reputation and character.
Here, name represents the son’s person and reputation.
4:15: This phrase, a restorer of life, refers to how Naomi will again experience joy and hope in her life as a result of having this grandson.
Here, old age represents Naomi when she is old.

In this culture, the number seven represented the idea of completeness or perfection. This is a way to praise Ruth for how she has provided for Naomi by bearing a grandson for her by Boaz, when Naomi’s husband and sons could not provide for her because they had died.
4:16: The phrase And Naomi took the child does not mean that she took him away from Ruth in any hostile way. This probably indicates that Naomi held the child for a kind of ceremony of adoption.
4:17: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The first phrase introduces the naming event, and the second repeats it in order to report the event.
Here the term father specifically refers to a male parent.
Though King is not stated, it was clear to the original audience that this David was King David.
4:19: Hezron, Ram, and Amminidab are the names of men.
4:20: Amminidab, Nahshon, and Salmon are the names of men.
